title_en: Zhang Yu and Zhang Xia v. Shanghai Yalu Industrial Investment Co., Ltd. — dispute over pre-sale contract for commercial housing
ruling_gist_en: A liability limitation standard term is essentially a risk transfer agreement. In accordance with the principle of good faith, at the time of contract signing, in addition to prominently drawing attention to the content of the term, the business operator shall also truthfully inform the counterparty of major risks that have already manifested within the scope of exemption, so as to protect the counterparty's reliance interest. If the business operator intentionally conceals major risks, causing the counterparty to reach an exemption agreement under conditions of information asymmetry, it shall be deemed that the counterparty's true expression of intent does not include undertaking the concealed major risks, and the scope of the exemption agreement is limited to uncertain risks arising after contract signing. During subsequent performance, if a breach of contract ultimately occurs due to the malicious concealment of major risks, and the business operator seeks to apply the exemption clause to exclude its own liability for breach, the people's court shall not support such an argument.

full_text_en:
Zhang Yu and Zhang Xia v. Shanghai Yalu Industrial Investment Co., Ltd.

— Dispute over Commodity Housing Pre-sale Contract

【Ruling Summary】

A liability-limiting standard clause is essentially a risk transfer agreement. In accordance with the principle of good faith, at the time of signing the contract, the operator must not only prominently highlight the content of the clause but also truthfully inform the other party of any major risks that have already become apparent within the scope of the disclaimer, so as to protect the relying interests of the counterparty. If the operator intentionally conceals a major risk, causing the counterparty to reach a disclaimer agreement under information asymmetry, it shall be determined that the true expression of intention of the counterparty does not include assuming the concealed major risk, and the scope of the disclaimer agreement is limited to uncertain risks arising after the signing of the contract. In subsequent performance, if the breach of contract ultimately occurs due to the malicious concealment of a major risk, and the operator claims that the disclaimer clause excludes its own liability for breach of contract, the people's court shall not support such claim.

**Plaintiff:** Zhang Yu, male, 41 years old, residing in Susong County, Anqing City, Anhui Province.

**Plaintiff:** Zhang Xia, female, 39 years old, residing in Susong County, Anqing City, Anhui Province.

**Defendant:** Shanghai Yalu Industrial Investment Co., Ltd., domiciled at Mingxing Village, Jinhui Town, Fengxian District, Shanghai.

**Legal Representative:** Li Zhong, Chairman of the Company.

The plaintiffs Zhang Yu and Zhang Xia filed a lawsuit with the Fengxian District People's Court of Shanghai against the defendant Shanghai Yalu Industrial Investment Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Yalu Company) regarding a dispute over a commodity housing pre-sale contract.

The plaintiffs Zhang Yu and Zhang Xia alleged: In 2015, the parties signed the "Shanghai Commodity Housing Pre-sale Contract" for the purchase of property at Room 102, 1st Floor, Lane 5, Lane 128, Sub-lane 119, Taiqing Road, Fengxian District. The contract stipulated a total price of RMB 1,616,228 and required the defendant Yalu Company to deliver the property by December 31, 2015. Thereafter, Zhang Yu and Zhang Xia paid the down payment as agreed and arranged a mortgage loan according to the actual situation. However, Yalu Company did not deliver the property on time but delayed until July 1, 2016, before delivering it to the plaintiffs. At the time of handover, Zhang Yu and Zhang Xia requested Yalu Company to fulfill its obligation to pay for the delayed delivery, but Yalu Company said it would discuss further and has not responded to date. The plaintiffs requested the court to order Yalu Company to pay liquidated damages for delayed delivery of the property amounting to RMB 58,185 (all subsequent amounts are in RMB unless otherwise specified).

The defendant Yalu Company argued: The actual delivery date was indeed July 1, 2016. Although the delivery was delayed, the contract stipulated that in the event of force majeure, the time periods for delivery, obtaining the main property certificate, and applying for the individual property certificate would be postponed accordingly. During the actual construction of the property, force majeure situations occurred involving the installation and connection of riverside roads and public gas pipelines within the community, and the relevant authorities issued corresponding certificates. Yalu Company actively fulfilled its delivery obligation after the situation was resolved. Yalu Company did not breach the contract and should not bear liability for breach.

The Fengxian District People's Court of Shanghai found at first instance:

On August 15, 2015, the plaintiffs Zhang Yu and Zhang Xia signed the disputed pre-sale contract with the defendant Yalu Company, stipulating: Zhang Yu and Zhang Xia purchased from Yalu Company the property located at Room 102, 1st Floor, Lane 5, Lane 128, Sub-lane 119, Taiqing Highway, Fengxian District, Shanghai (hereinafter referred to as the disputed property), with a provisional total purchase price of RMB 1,616,228; Yalu Company was to deliver the property before December 31, 2015, except in cases of force majeure; if Yalu Company breached by failing to deliver on time, it would pay liquidated damages at a daily rate of 0.02% of the purchase price paid. In Supplementary Clause I of the contract, Article 11 was amended and supplemented as follows: Party A (Yalu Company) shall deliver the property to Party B (Zhang Yu and Zhang Xia) before December 31, 2015, except in cases of force majeure and other objective circumstances difficult for Yalu Company to anticipate, including but not limited to: delays in the installation of public supporting facilities such as water supply, power supply, gas, drainage, communications, internet, and roads; project delays caused by planning adjustments; changes in government policies, etc. It was also stipulated that in the event of force majeure, the time periods for delivery, obtaining the main property certificate, and applying for the individual property certificate under this contract would be postponed accordingly; the scope of force majeure referred to in this contract included natural disasters, civil unrest, severe weather, government actions, approval and installation of municipal supporting facilities, major engineering technical difficulties, and other events or situations that could not be foreseen, avoided, controlled, or overcome. Thereafter, Zhang Yu and Zhang Xia paid the purchase price in installments. In June 2016, Yalu Company issued a move-in notice confirming: the total measured purchase price was RMB 1,604,177.84, with a refund of RMB 12,050.16; Zhang Yu and Zhang Xia were required to complete the move-in procedures on July 1, 2016. On July 1, 2016, Zhang Yu and Zhang Xia and Yalu Company completed the handover procedures. Zhang Yu and Zhang Xia believed that Yalu Company had delayed delivery, leading to the lawsuit.

The external gas pipeline project for the community where the disputed property is located was contracted by the Jinhui Town People's Government of Fengxian District, Shanghai, with a gas company on March 23, 2015, with a construction period of 90 days. Due to local villagers blocking the construction by demanding urban social insurance for the use of land for pipeline construction and supporting road construction within the community, the project could not be completed on schedule. On February 16, 2016, the Jinhui Town People's Government held a coordination meeting to resolve the issue, and the project proceeded smoothly. On April 20, 2016, the external gas pipeline project was completed and accepted. On May 9, 2016, the gas company issued a certificate of conformity. On June 2, 2016, the defendant Yalu Company obtained the Shanghai Urban and Rural Planning Construction Project Planning Acceptance Certificate. On July 1, 2016, Yalu Company obtained the Shanghai New Residential Building Delivery Permit.

During the first-instance trial, the defendant Yalu Company insisted that it should not bear liability for breach of contract, but considering the specific circumstances, it voluntarily agreed to compensate the plaintiffs Zhang Yu and Zhang Xia in the amount of RMB 11,757.

The Fengxian District People's Court of Shanghai held at first instance:

A legally established contract is binding on the parties. In this case, the disputed pre-sale contract signed between the plaintiffs Zhang Yu and Zhang Xia and the defendant Yalu Company was the true expression of intention of both parties, legal and valid, and both parties should abide by it. The actual delivery date in this case was July 1, 2016, which exceeded the delivery period stipulated in the contract. However, the reason for the delayed delivery of the disputed property was primarily due to factors such as municipal supporting facilities. Article 15 of Supplementary Clause I of the contract stipulated that if delivery was delayed due to government actions, municipal supporting projects, etc., the delivery time would be postponed accordingly. Zhang Yu and Zhang Xia argued that the delay in supporting facilities did not constitute force majeure. The first-instance court held that although the delay in municipal supporting facilities did not fall within the legal scope of force majeure, it was indeed a situation beyond the control of the developer. Articles 8 and 15 of Supplementary Clause I stipulated that, in addition to force majeure, objective circumstances difficult for Yalu Company to anticipate were included, with examples such as delays in municipal supporting facilities. In this case, it was precisely this situation that led to the delay in delivery, so the delivery time could be postponed. Moreover, Yalu Company fulfilled its delivery obligation on the same day it obtained the relevant permits. Therefore, Zhang Yu and Zhang Xia's claim that Yalu Company should bear liability for delayed delivery lacked basis and was not accepted. Zhang Yu and Zhang Xia also argued that the contract was a standard-form contract, but the supplementary clauses of the disputed pre-sale contract were not non-negotiable at the time of signing and did not constitute standard clauses. Even if they did constitute standard clauses, they did not fall within the invalid standard clauses as provided by law. Since Yalu Company voluntarily agreed to compensate Zhang Yu and Zhang Xia for their losses, this was not contrary to law, and the first-instance court supported it.

Accordingly, the Fengxian District People's Court of Shanghai, in accordance with Article 8 of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China, Article 64, Paragraph 1, and Article 253 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, rendered a judgment on May 12, 2017:

1. Rejecting all claims of the plaintiffs Zhang Yu and Zhang Xia;

2. The defendant Shanghai Yalu Industrial Investment Co., Ltd. shall compensate the plaintiffs Zhang Yu and Zhang Xia in the amount of RMB 11,757 within ten days from the date the judgment takes effect.

Zhang Yu and Zhang Xia, dissatisfied with the first-instance judgment, appealed to the Shanghai No. 1 Intermediate People's Court, arguing:

1. The parties signed the "Shanghai Commodity Housing Pre-sale Contract" (hereinafter referred to as the disputed pre-sale contract) on August 15, 2015. The supplementary clauses of the contract expanded the definition of "force majeure" by listing delays in municipal supporting facilities as within the scope of the appellee Yalu Company's disclaimer. This disclaimer clause was clearly unfair to them, and Yalu Company did not fulfill its duty to draw attention to it at the time of signing. Therefore, this disclaimer clause should be an invalid standard clause.

2. The letter dated March 27, 2015, provided by Yalu Company indicated that as of the date of the letter, Yalu Company was already aware of the actual risk of delay in the supporting facilities. Yalu Company did not inform the purchasers of this situation at the time of signing and still promised to deliver the property by December 31, 2015. Even if the disclaimer clause were valid, it could not be applied to this case. The appeal requested: reversal of the first-instance judgment, and a revised judgment ordering Yalu Company to pay liquidated damages for delayed delivery in the amount of RMB 58,185.

On August 22, 2017, the appellants Zhang Yu and Zhang Xia submitted a written opinion to the second-instance court, stating that they requested the second-instance court to determine the amount of liquidated damages at 55% of their appeal claim, waiving the remaining 45%.

The appellee Yalu Company argued that the delay in delivering the disputed property was entirely due to the delay in municipal supporting facility construction. The location of these works was outside the land parcel transferred to Yalu Company. The delay was caused by the local government's failure to timely coordinate conflicts with residents, which could not be attributed to Yalu Company. The construction within the scope contracted by Yalu Company was completed in 2015. The disclaimer clause in the supplementary clauses was valid, and the circumstances of this case met the conditions for its application. Yalu Company should not pay liquidated damages. The first-instance judgment was correct, and the second-instance court was requested to affirm it.

The Shanghai No. 1 Intermediate People's Court confirmed the facts found at first instance and additionally found:

The appellee Yalu Company obtained the pre-sale permit for the community where the disputed property is located in 2014. On March 27, 2015, Yalu Company sent a letter to the Jinhui Town People's Government of Fengxian District, Shanghai, stating: There is currently no external gas pipe interface or external water pipe interface outside the red line of the plot. The supporting facilities outside the red line of the community should be resolved by the town government; otherwise, it would affect Yalu Company's ability to deliver the property on time. In August 2015, Yalu Company completed the construction work within the community area where the disputed property is located.

The second-instance court also found that Article 8, Paragraph 2 of the Supplementary Clauses of the disputed pre-sale contract provided: In the event of the above situations, it shall not be considered as Party A's delayed delivery, but Party A shall promptly notify Party B of these objective circumstances.

It was further found that the "Meeting Minutes" dated December 30, 2015, submitted by the appellee Yalu Company, recorded: The gas company originally planned to start construction after the New Year holiday on the 4th, laying pipes from the west side of the community. The "Meeting Minutes" dated February 16, 2016, recorded the topic as: Resolving the issue of uncollected land outside the red line of the residential project, and villagers obstructing the construction of roads and pipelines outside the red line.

During the second-instance trial, the appellee Yalu Company stated: 1. The contract text provided to purchasers contained two delivery deadlines: one was September 2015, and the other was December 2015. 2. On March 27, 2015, Yalu Company learned that residents were obstructing the gas supporting facility construction and therefore sent a letter urging the government department, but at that time it was not certain that this would cause a delay in completion, as there was still a possibility of catching up later.

In response, the court held that, first, the appellee Yalü Company knew that completion of ancillary works was a prerequisite for the overall completion acceptance inspection and should have kept close track of the specific progress of the ancillary works to thereby predict the actual date on which the houses could be delivered. The government authority signed the contract with the ancillary works contractor on March 23, 2015. According to Yalü Company's statements and relevant evidence, because the land for the construction plot had not yet been expropriated, disputes existed between local residents and the government authority, who obstructed construction, causing the ancillary works to be unable to commence and to become stalled. On March 27 of the same year, after learning of this situation, Yalü Company sent a letter to the government authority urging action, but as of August 2015, there were no signs that the obstruction by residents could be eliminated. It was not until December 30, 2015, that the ancillary works contractor was still unable to determine the actual construction start date at a coordination meeting. If the stalled state continued, it would inevitably delay completion of the overall project. Therefore, although "delay in ancillary works leading to overdue delivery of houses" was not yet a certain fact as of March 27, 2015, it was no longer an abstract theoretical possibility but a significant existing risk known to Yalü Company.

Second, the delivery deadline is an important factor for homebuyers in deciding whether to purchase a property. Without receiving a risk warning, homebuyers are unable to effectively assess the practical feasibility of the delivery deadline, placing them in a state of information asymmetry at the time of contracting. Although the appellee Yalü Company hoped that the obstacles could be eliminated during subsequent performance, the construction stagnation caused by the land expropriation issue was a fundamental delaying factor. This factor was not within Yalü Company's subjective control, and according to common sense, land expropriation requires procedures prescribed by law and cannot be resolved quickly in a short period. Given the substantial uncertainty in the actual feasibility of the delivery deadline, Yalü Company's act of concealing the risk could cause actual losses to the homebuyers' reliance interests. Accordingly, Yalü Company could not exempt itself from its disclosure obligation on the ground that it might later catch up with the schedule. The court determined that Yalü Company owed a duty to disclose the risk of delay in ancillary works to all homebuyers who signed contracts from March 27, 2015. The subject pre-sale contract was signed on August 15, 2015. Yalü Company failed to disclose the corresponding risk to the appellants Zhang Yu and Zhang Xia, thereby violating the disclosure obligation agreed upon in the contract.

Third, the issue is whether Yalü Company's concealment of the risk resulted in the exclusion of the application of the disputed liability limitation clause.

The disputed liability limitation clause does not expressly impose a time restriction on the occurrence of the exempting events. The appellants Zhang Yu and Zhang Xia argued that, given Yalü Company's concealment of the delay risk, the agreed exempting events could only apply to circumstances arising after the signing of the contract and should not apply to this case. This is a restrictive interpretation of the contract clause. Yalü Company argued that the time of occurrence of the risk event should not affect the scope of the exemption, and that the disputed liability limitation clause should apply to this case, which is a basic understanding based on the literal meaning of the contract.

The essence of the dispute between the parties on this issue is a difference in interpretation of the contract clause in the context of Yalü Company's concealment of a known risk. Article 41 of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter "Contract Law") provides that where a dispute arises over the understanding of a standard term, it shall be interpreted in accordance with the ordinary understanding. Where there are two or more interpretations of a standard term, an interpretation unfavorable to the party providing the standard term shall prevail. Paragraph 1 of Article 125 provides that where a dispute arises between the parties over the understanding of a contract clause, the true meaning of that clause shall be determined in accordance with the words and expressions used in the contract, the relevant provisions of the contract, the purpose of the contract, trade usage, and the principle of good faith. Based on the above rules for interpreting standard terms, the court analyzes the issue as follows:

(1) A pre-sale contract for commercial housing is a contract for the sale of commercial housing under construction. Different homebuyers sign contracts at different times corresponding to different stages of construction progress. Homebuyers are not aware of the specific progress and lack the ability to assess the feasibility of the delivery deadline. Moreover, the delivery deadline clause is also a standard term unilaterally drafted by the appellee Yalü Company, which could adjust the delivery deadline based on actual construction progress at the time of signing. In this case, Yalü Company also acknowledged that the delivery deadlines set in its pre-sale contracts were divided into two types: September 2015 and December 2015, indicating that it had already replanned the delivery deadline in subsequent sales based on the progress of the ancillary works. Therefore, in the absence of being informed of an existing real risk, the agreement on liability limitation reached between the homebuyers and Yalü Company was based on the homebuyers' reliance on the realistic reasonableness of the delivery deadline.

(2) Since the appellee Yalü Company unilaterally concealed the real risk of delay and had the ability to replan the delivery deadline, the homebuyers had reason to believe that Yalü Company had made a commitment regarding the practical feasibility of the delivery deadline: that the deadline had fully taken into account the actual progress conditions known to Yalü Company, that the original risk events could be eliminated in a timely manner, and that if no new exempting events occurred during subsequent performance, delivery could be achieved within that deadline. Therefore, the appellants Zhang Yu and Zhang Xia's argument that the scope of risk transfer agreed upon by the parties was directed at risk events arising during subsequent performance and should not include the actual conditions that had already been incorporated into the consideration factors for the delivery deadline is consistent with the principle of good faith interpretation under Article 125 of the Contract Law.

(3) There is a conflict between the parties' understanding of the standard contract clauses. According to the rule of interpretation in favor of the counterparty provided in Article 41 of the Contract Law, the court holds that the value of the homebuyers' reliance interest under the principle of good faith outweighs the interest of the provider of the standard term, the appellee Yalü Company, in limiting its liability risk. The complementary logical relationship between the delivery deadline clause and the disputed liability limitation clause should be interpreted as follows: the scope of application of the disputed liability limitation clause is limited to uncertain risk events occurring after the signing of the contract and cannot apply to real risk events that were concealed at the time of signing. The court does not accept Yalü Company's argument that its concealment of the risk does not affect the application of the disputed liability limitation clause.

(4) In this case, the appellee Yalü Company knew as early as March 27, 2015, that the ancillary works were obstructed and stalled, creating a real risk of delay. However, when signing the contract on August 15, 2015, it did not disclose this risk event to the appellants Zhang Yu and Zhang Xia, but instead promised to deliver the houses by December 31, 2015. The real risk of obstruction and delay of the ancillary works arose before the signing of the subject pre-sale contract. In the absence of any new risk events arising subsequently, the original risk state continued to extend, ultimately resulting in the delivery of the subject houses on July 1, 2016. Yalü Company's above conduct breached its commitment that the delivery deadline was practically feasible and is not entitled to assert the application of the disputed liability limitation clause on the ground of delay in ancillary works.

Based on the above reasons, the appellee Yalü Company's assertion that the disputed liability limitation clause should apply in this case on the ground of delay in ancillary works, as a defense against the appellants Zhang Yu and Zhang Xia's claim for liquidated damages for overdue delivery, lacks factual and legal basis, and the court does not support it. Zhang Yu and Zhang Xia's claim that Yalü Company should bear liquidated damages for overdue delivery is consistent with the contract, and the court supports it. According to the subject pre-sale contract, the total overdue period for Yalü Company was 183 days. Calculated at 0.02% per day of the total house price of RMB 1,604,177.84 based on the measured area, the liquidated damages total RMB 58,713. At the second instance, Zhang Yu and Zhang Xia voluntarily stated that they would claim liquidated damages at 55% of the standard agreed in the contract. This is a disposition of their own rights, not contrary to law, and is also commensurate with Yalü Company's actual fault. The court permits this. Accordingly, the court determines that Yalü Company shall pay Zhang Yu and Zhang Xia liquidated damages for overdue delivery in the amount of RMB 32,292.15.

In conclusion, in accordance with Article 41, Paragraph 1 of Article 125 of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China, Article 9 of the Interpretation (II) of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Application of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China, and Item (2) of Paragraph 1 of Article 170 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the Shanghai No. 1 Intermediate People's Court rendered the following judgment on August 28, 2017:

1. Set aside the civil judgment (2017) Hu 0120 Min Chu No. 4598 of the Fengxian District People's Court of Shanghai;

2. The appellee Shanghai Yalü Industrial Investment Co., Ltd. shall, within ten days after this judgment takes effect, pay the appellants Zhang Yu and Zhang Xia liquidated damages for overdue delivery in the amount of RMB 32,292.15.

This judgment is final.
